meta.theme: manners as moral practice rather than decoration: a manner claims nothing about feeling, which is why it can make consideration reliable, and why an arbitrary code can still be judged by whether it puts a stranger at ease

meta.reviewer_notes: Two objections are conceded at length before the turn, so the passage reads for two paragraphs as an attack on its own thesis. The set is built to catch readers who stop at either concession, and the scope question checks whether the reader kept the narrowed version at the end. 2026-10-03 CAT-size pass: 610→500 words, 5→5 paragraphs, 6→4 questions. Every paragraph carries a move (two charges, two answers, the thesis), so none was dropped; tightened each paragraph instead. Kept main idea, paragraph function, inference and implication; dropped the phrase-in-context and scope questions, which shared paragraphs with the kept ones.

quality.adversarial_review: All four options in the main-idea question now open on the same concession, so the concession certifies nothing and the question is decided entirely by the clause after 'but'. Three readings then run through the paper. The shadow is the reply mistaken for the argument: the case for manners is that a manner makes no claim about feeling and so cannot be a lie, with everything after that taken for illustration. It holds an option in every question (Q1 'the decisive reply', Q2 'bound to mean it', Q4 'tells its recipient nothing whatever', Q5 'no use of a code can be dishonest', Q6 'leaves open whether such an act has any value') and it dies on the opening of the fourth paragraph, 'That is the whole argument', which is placed after the hypocrisy reply and before the case about mood, and on the closing paragraph's counterfeit, which is a dishonest use of a code by a performer who has claimed nothing. The second rival ranks habit above feeling and lets manners displace judgement; the fourth paragraph blocks it twice, calling manners 'the part of this work that has been decided in advance' and ending 'This is not a substitute for morality', and it calls the person moved to kindness pleasant company rather than a lesser person. The third rival keeps the first charge at full strength and confines the defence to the community that inherited the code; the last paragraph denies exactly that, since what is arbitrary is the code and not the practice, and attending to another's comfort is 'recognisable across every code that has one'. The paragraph-function question has been re-cut so that its key names the paragraph's move, deriving dependability from the cost of deciding afresh, rather than restating the thesis the main-idea key already carries. Strength parity was imposed across the set afterwards: no distractor in this file is quantified more strongly than its key, because a single overreaching option was found to condemn the whole reading it belonged to without the passage being read. (2026-10-03, CAT-size pass: q2, q6 were dropped, so any note above about them no longer applies.)

paragraphs.text: The case against manners is strong and should be made first. Codes of etiquette are arbitrary: which fork, which greeting, how long to wait. They are local, and they change. Worse, an elaborate, unwritten code is an excellent instrument for sorting people, since it can be learned only by growing up among those who already have it. Anyone who has watched a room enjoy a newcomer's hesitation over a table knows that manners have served cruelty as faithfully as kindness. None of this is exaggerated, and nothing that follows denies it.

A second charge is the one most people feel more strongly: manners are mere form. The courteous act is performed whether or not it is meant, and a performance that is not meant is a small lie. On this view manners at best decorate a good character and at worst disguise a bad one, and honesty means behaving as you feel.

The second charge is the easier to answer, and answering it makes the first answerable too. Consider a tired host, longing to be alone, whose guest has arrived early. The host rises, takes the coat and offers the chair with the better light. None of this is a lie, because none of it is a statement. The host has not claimed to be delighted. Hypocrisy is the claim of a feeling one does not have; a manner claims nothing about feeling at all. It is an action offered to another person, and what makes it valuable is precisely that it did not have to be felt.

That is the whole argument. Morality asks us to take others into account, and doing that from scratch each time is expensive: it requires noticing, weighing and deciding, and nobody has that much attention to spend on an ordinary Tuesday. Manners are the part of this work that has been decided in advance. They turn consideration from something one must summon into something one already does, which matters most on the days when it would not have been summoned. A person who is kind whenever moved to be kind is pleasant company and cannot be relied upon. A person with manners has made a promise that their mood is not consulted about. This is not a substitute for morality. It is the form morality takes when it must work every day, among people one does not particularly love.

The first charge survives, but narrowed. What is arbitrary is the code, not the practice. Whether one rises or bows is local accident; attending to another's comfort before one's own convenience is not, and it is recognisable across every code that has one. That is also the test of a code used badly. The same rule can be applied to put a stranger at ease or to establish that he does not know it, and these are not two styles of good manners but the practice and its counterfeit. Nothing in the code itself tells you which is happening. Everything in the situation does.

questions.target_mistake: reading the concession every option makes as evidence about which option is right, and then taking the reply about hypocrisy, the ranking of habit over feeling, or the surviving charge for the case the concession is clearing ground for
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: both charges against manners are granted, and the passage still concludes that manners are moral practice because they make consideration independent of mood.
questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Codes of manners are arbitrary and have been misused, but the practice offers no standard of its own, so a code is best judged by those who keep it.
options.B: The charge that manners are mere form is the one that matters, and it fails: a manner makes no claim about what its performer feels.
options.C: Settled habit is a surer guide to conduct than feeling, which is why a person does better not to wait on their sympathies.
options.D: Codes of manners are arbitrary and have been misused, but manners themselves are moral practice, since they make consideration reliable by putting it beyond the reach of mood.

explanation.expert_notice: The passage lays out two charges and answers them in the reverse of the order it states them. The second charge, that manners are mere form, is answered in the third paragraph; the first, that codes are arbitrary and have been misused, is answered only in the fifth, and the fourth paragraph in between opens 'That is the whole argument'.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option holds the concession and the claim together in the order the passage does. It grants that codes are arbitrary and have been misused, which is the first paragraph and the last, and then states the thesis in the passage's own terms: manners are moral practice because they make consideration reliable when feeling would not have supplied it. The test to apply to every candidate is which claim the ground is being cleared for, and the fourth paragraph names it when it opens 'That is the whole argument' and then talks about a mood that is not consulted.
explanation.question_type_note: In a concession-thesis passage the main idea is the claim the concessions were made for. Conceding is what the author does first, so an option that concedes is not thereby the author's, and an option that does not concede is not thereby a distractor.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage opens against itself, mark where the concessions stop. Everything before that mark is other people's case, and an option that lands back inside that material is describing the setup rather than the argument.

distractors.why_wrong: The last paragraph exists to deny the middle clause. What is arbitrary is the code and not the practice, and attending to another's comfort before one's own convenience 'is recognisable across every code that has one', which supplies precisely the standard this option says the practice lacks, and supplies it to an outsider as readily as to a member.
distractors.seductive_element: The charge is made with real force in the first paragraph and never taken back, so an option that concedes and then lets the charge stand reads as the balanced verdict.

distractors.why_wrong: It stops at the third paragraph's reply to one objection, which the passage treats as clearing the ground rather than as the case: the next paragraph opens 'That is the whole argument' and what follows is about reliability, not about sincerity. The passage also ranks the two charges the other way, calling the first the one that 'should be made first' and answering it last.
distractors.seductive_element: The reply is the most quotable sentence in the passage and entirely true of it, and the passage does say this is the charge most people feel more strongly.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage recommends nothing about the sympathies. It calls a person moved to kindness 'pleasant company' and merely unreliable, and it says manners are the form morality takes rather than a better guide than feeling. Nothing in it tells anyone what to do about what they feel.
distractors.seductive_element: The contrast between a mood that is not consulted and a kindness that waits to be moved does sound as though it were building towards advice about the feelings.

questions.target_mistake: offering the paragraph's opening premise or its closing guard as the work the paragraph is doing, or converting a claim about dependability into a ranking of habit above feeling
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: this paragraph takes the cost of deciding afresh on every occasion and turns it into a reason why an action already decided can be depended on.
questions.stem: The fourth paragraph primarily serves to

options.A: set out how much attention taking other people into account would need if it were done from scratch
options.B: restate the charge that manners are mere form in the author's own vocabulary
options.C: derive what a manner is worth from the expense of producing consideration on demand
options.D: concede that manners are no substitute for the morality whose form they take

explanation.expert_notice: The paragraph is a derivation with its premise first. Taking people into account from scratch each time 'is expensive: it requires noticing, weighing and deciding, and nobody has that much attention to spend on an ordinary Tuesday.' Everything after that sentence is what follows from it.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names the move the paragraph makes. The expense is not raised as a complaint about how tiring consideration is; it is raised to explain why consideration cannot be produced on demand, from which the paragraph derives what a manner is worth: the deciding was done earlier, so the action survives a day on which nobody would have summoned it. The two people set side by side at the end make the derivation visible, separating being pleasant from being able to be counted on.
explanation.question_type_note: A paragraph-function question asks what a paragraph does with its material, not what its most quotable sentence says. Premises and guards are both easy to mistake for the point.
explanation.reading_habit: In a paragraph that carries an argument, name the premise and the conclusion separately before you look at the options. An option that reports the premise is describing the ground the paragraph stands on, not the work it does.

distractors.why_wrong: The expense is real and is stated here, but it is the premise the paragraph argues from rather than the thing it argues; every sentence after it is about what manners do with that expense, and the paragraph ends on what can be relied upon rather than on how tiring consideration is.
distractors.seductive_element: It reports the paragraph's second sentence accurately, and a claim you can point to in the text feels like an answer.

distractors.why_wrong: The charge that manners are mere form belongs to the second paragraph and was answered in the third; the fourth opens 'That is the whole argument' and builds a positive case out of what consideration costs. Nothing in it restates an objection, and the objection it might restate has already been disposed of.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph does talk about what a manner does rather than about what it feels, which sounds like the sincerity question still being worked through.

distractors.why_wrong: The sentence is there, but it guards the claim rather than being it, and it is not a concession at all: the paragraph opens 'That is the whole argument', which locates the paragraph's business in the argument the guard protects.
distractors.seductive_element: It sits in the paragraph's closing lines, and a reader who remembers endings better than middles will take the last qualification for the point.

questions.target_mistake: restoring the ordinary assumption that a courtesy is worth more when it is felt, or over-extending the claim that a manner makes no claim about feeling into a claim that it reveals nothing
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that any supported inference will keep feeling out of the assessment, since the passage locates value in the action being offered rather than in the state of the person offering it.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A courtesy performed without warmth is worth less than the same courtesy performed with it.
options.B: A courteous act leaves its recipient without evidence of the performer's state of mind.
options.C: Any practice performed from habit is more valuable than the same practice performed from feeling.
options.D: A courtesy performed reluctantly is not, for that reason, worth less than one performed gladly.

explanation.expert_notice: Two sentences set the terms of value. In the third paragraph, 'what makes it valuable is precisely that it did not have to be felt'; in the fourth, the person to be relied on is the one whose mood 'is not consulted'. Feeling is not a cheap ingredient in this account; it is not an ingredient.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option follows from that. If a manner makes no claim about feeling, and its value lies in being available when feeling is absent, then the absence of warmth cannot by itself reduce what the act is worth. The option is carefully weak, not worth less for that reason, which is exactly the strength the passage supports, since it never says reluctance adds value either.
explanation.question_type_note: Inference questions test whether a reader can hold an author's revised standard instead of the one they arrived with; the trap is usually the ordinary opinion the passage has just argued against.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author detaches value from a familiar source, write the new standard down and judge every option by it. Options that quietly restore the old standard are the hardest to see, because they feel like common sense.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the view the third paragraph is written against; the passage locates the value of the act in its being offered at all, and says in terms that not having to be felt is what makes it valuable.
distractors.seductive_element: It is what almost everyone believes before reading, and the passage's own sympathy for the tired host makes warmth feel like the missing ingredient.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says a manner makes no claim about feeling, which is a point about what is asserted, not about what can be read. Hypocrisy is defined as 'the claim of a feeling one does not have', and the tired host is described in enough detail for a reader to see exactly what he feels while claiming nothing.
distractors.seductive_element: It is one short step from 'claims nothing about feeling' to 'shows nothing about feeling', and the step feels like the rigorous version of the author's point.

distractors.why_wrong: The claim covers manners, where the alternative is that nothing is done at all, and it never ranks habit above feeling as a general principle; the passage calls the person moved by kindness pleasant company, not a lesser person.
distractors.seductive_element: It generalises the passage's real contrast and sounds like the abstract statement of its principle.

questions.target_mistake: converting the author's test for how a code is used into a rule that conformity settles the matter, into a licence covering every use of a code, or into relativism about codes
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: since the same rule can be used either to put a stranger at ease or to expose him, following the code correctly cannot by itself settle whether someone is doing what manners are for.
questions.stem: Which of the following follows from the passage's closing paragraph?

options.A: Two people may follow the same code of manners and only one of them be doing what manners are for.
options.B: Since a manner makes no claim about feeling, no use of a code of manners can be dishonest.
options.C: A code followed from habit rather than feeling is the one kind that can be relied on anywhere.
options.D: Because codes of manners differ from one place to another, no one code can be judged better than the rest.

explanation.expert_notice: The last three sentences carry the whole implication: the same rule 'can be applied to put a stranger at ease or to establish that he does not know it', these are 'the practice and its counterfeit', and 'Nothing in the code itself tells you which is happening.' Conformity and purpose have been pulled apart.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that separation stated as a consequence. If the identical rule can serve the practice or its counterfeit, and the code cannot distinguish them, then two people can be observing the same etiquette faultlessly while only one is doing what manners exist to do. The passage adds where the difference is visible instead: everything in the situation tells you.
explanation.question_type_note: An implication question takes the author's claim one honest step. The trap takes three, usually by turning a criterion into a forecast or a recommendation.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what the final sentences make impossible rather than what they make likely. Here they make it impossible to read intention off conformity, and the answer is whatever states that impossibility.

distractors.why_wrong: The closing paragraph supplies the counter-instance itself. A rule applied 'to establish that he does not know it' is called the counterfeit of the practice, and it is performed by someone who has claimed no feeling at all; the reply about hypocrisy answers one charge and does not clear every use of a code.
distractors.seductive_element: It carries the passage's own most quotable defence into the last paragraph, and an argument extended one step past where the author left it feels like a consequence.

distractors.why_wrong: The final paragraph's point is that the code settles nothing: the same rule, followed just as habitually, can put a stranger at ease or expose him, and 'Nothing in the code itself tells you which is happening.' Reliability comes from what the practice is for, not from the fact that a code is being followed out of habit.
distractors.seductive_element: Habit is genuinely the passage's ground for dependability in the fourth paragraph, so carrying it into the fifth looks like consistency rather than a change of subject.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph exists to deny this. What is arbitrary is the code and not the practice, and attending to another's comfort is said to be recognisable across every code that has one, which supplies exactly the standard this option says is unavailable.
distractors.seductive_element: The first paragraph's insistence that codes are local and changeable reads like relativism if the final paragraph's correction is missed.

vocabulary.passage_use: Codes of etiquette are arbitrary: which fork, which greeting
vocabulary.meaning_here: settled by accident or convention rather than by any reason inherent in the thing

vocabulary.passage_use: from something one must summon into something one already does
vocabulary.meaning_here: to call up in oneself by an effort of will at the moment it is needed

vocabulary.passage_use: not two styles of good manners but the practice and its counterfeit
vocabulary.meaning_here: an imitation that keeps the outward form while doing the opposite work

mentor.challenge: For two paragraphs the author argues against the position the passage will defend. Decide where the concessions stop, because several options are built from the part where the author is agreeing with the other side.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Codes of manners really are arbitrary and really have been used cruelly, but a manner is not a lie about one's feelings and never claimed to be one, and its worth lies exactly there: it makes consideration available on the days when nobody feels like offering any.
mentor.main_idea: Manners are not decoration on a good character and not a disguise on a bad one. Because a courteous act says nothing about what the person feels, it cannot be a lie, and because it has been settled in advance it does not have to be summoned. That makes consideration reliable. The rules themselves are local and changeable, and they can be turned into a way of catching people out, which is not manners but its counterfeit.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Start with everything wrong with manners. The rules are made up: which fork, which greeting, how long to wait. None of it had to be that way, and it keeps changing. Worse, an unwritten code is a very good way to sort people, because you can only learn it by growing up among those who already know it. Anyone who has seen a room enjoy a newcomer freezing at a table knows this.

Then there is the other complaint, the one people feel more strongly. Manners are just form. You do the polite thing whether or not you mean it, and pretending is a small lie.

The writer answers the second complaint first. Picture a tired host who wants to be alone and whose guest turns up early. The host stands, takes the coat, points to the chair with the better light. None of that is a lie, because none of it is a claim. The host never said 'I am delighted'. Lying about a feeling is hypocrisy; a manner does not mention feelings at all. And here is the surprise: the fact that it did not have to be felt is what makes it worth something.

Now the main point. Being moral means taking other people into account. Doing that from scratch every time is expensive: you have to notice, weigh and decide, and nobody has that much attention on an ordinary day. Manners are the bit that has already been decided. They turn consideration from something you have to work up into something you simply do, and that matters most on the days you would not have worked it up. Someone who is kind whenever they feel kind is nice to be around and cannot be relied on. Someone with manners has made a promise that their mood does not get a vote.

Finally, back to the first complaint, now smaller. The rules are arbitrary; the practice is not. Bow or rise, it does not matter: putting someone else's comfort before your own convenience is recognisable everywhere. And that is how you spot the abuse. The very same rule can be used to make a stranger comfortable or to show that he does not know it. Those are not two kinds of good manners. One is the real thing and the other is a fake. The rule will not tell you which; the situation will.
mentor.why_difficult: Much of the passage is spent agreeing with the other side, and both concessions are made in strong, quotable language. A reader who samples the first two paragraphs comes away with the impression that the passage attacks manners, and the questions are full of options taken from exactly those paragraphs. The turn is then unusual: instead of denying that manners are mere form, the author accepts that they are form and argues that form is the point. Readers who expect a defence of sincerity have to give up the standard they came in with, which is harder than following a new idea.
mentor.author_intention: To take the two strongest objections seriously enough that the defence cannot be dismissed as sentimental, and then to move the value of manners from the feelings behind them to their reliability.

paragraph_journey.note: Rules of etiquette are made up, local and changeable, and an unwritten code is a fine tool for humiliating outsiders. The author says none of this is exaggerated.
The other complaint: manners are empty form, and a courtesy that is not meant is a small lie. On that view honesty means acting as you feel.
The tired host who greets an early guest is not lying, because nothing has been claimed. Hypocrisy is a false claim about feeling; a manner makes no claim about feeling.
Considering others from scratch each time costs attention nobody has. Manners are the part decided beforehand, so consideration survives a bad mood. That is reliability, not decoration.
What is arbitrary is the code, not the practice. The same rule can put a stranger at ease or expose him, and only the situation shows which is happening.

mentor.tone_progression: Frank and almost hostile while the objections are being made, then quietly confident as the reply is set out, and finally exact: the last paragraph gives ground and takes it back in the same breath, ending on two short sentences instead of a summary.
key_transitions: 'None of this is exaggerated, and nothing that follows denies it.' (end of paragraph 1): the concession is sealed rather than withdrawn.
'Hypocrisy is the claim of a feeling one does not have; a manner claims nothing about feeling at all.' (paragraph 3): the objection is dissolved by a distinction.
'That is the whole argument.' (opening of paragraph 4): the thesis finally arrives.
mentor.misunderstanding: Hurried readers build one of two pictures. In the first, the passage is a criticism of etiquette, because that is what the opening paragraph is and it is written with more energy than anything else in the piece. In the second, the passage is a defence of sincerity, in which good manners are valuable when they express real feeling; that reading survives only until the third paragraph, which says the opposite, but it survives long enough to make the inference question look easy. Both mistakes come from reading the passage's topic rather than its argument.
mentor.traps_summary: The options in this set are drawn mostly from two places: the conceded objections in the first half, and the ordinary opinions a reader brings in. Expect the concession dressed as the thesis, the ordinary view of sincerity dressed as an inference, and the author's criterion inflated into a forecast or a recommendation. The cure in each case is to ask which paragraph is speaking and whether it is speaking for the author.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage opens by making the case against itself, find the sentence that closes the concession and mark it. Everything before it can be true, well written and quotable while being no part of the author's position, and examiners build their most attractive wrong options from exactly that material. The author's claim begins where the agreeing stops.
mentor.real_world: The same question arrives whenever someone says they will not attend a ceremony they do not believe in, or that they would rather be honest than polite: the passage suggests asking not what the gesture expresses, but what it makes available to the other person.
mentor.takeaway: A manner is a promise that your mood does not get a vote.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of your kindnesses would survive a week in which you did not feel like being kind?

eli10.big_idea: The rules of politeness are made up, but manners are a real part of being good: kindness decided beforehand, so moods cannot cancel it.
eli10.story: Some people attack manners. The rules are made up and keep changing. Worse, unwritten rules can make newcomers feel small. The writer agrees. A second complaint is that manners are fake: smiling without meaning it is a small lie. Picture a tired host whose guest comes early. The host takes the coat and offers the best chair. That is not a lie, because the host never said 'I am happy'. A manner makes no claim about feelings. Now the main point. Being kind from scratch every time takes effort, and nobody has that much on an ordinary day. Manners are kindness decided beforehand. So you still say 'good morning' on a grumpy day, and your mood does not get a vote. Finally, the rules are made up, but caring about others is not. The same rule can welcome a stranger or embarrass him. Only the situation shows which.
paragraphs: Grants the first charge: the rules are made up, keep changing and can be used to shame outsiders.
States the second charge: manners are empty form, and politeness you do not mean is a small lie.
Answers it with a tired host: a manner claims nothing about feelings, so it is no lie.
Gives the main point: manners are consideration decided in advance, so moods cannot switch it off.
Narrows the first charge: the rules are arbitrary, the caring is not, and misuse shows in the situation.
eli10.author_view: The writer is fair to the critics, then calmly confident: manners matter precisely because they do not depend on how we feel.
